---
title: "Causal graphs and adjustment sets"
subtitle: "Confounders, mediators, colliders and selection"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
outcomes <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_outcomes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
no_thirds <- readr::read_csv("../data/housing_emails.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_any(c(pop_third, poverty_third, black_third, hispanic_third), is.na)) |>
  nrow()

fmt <- \(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
out <- \(o, cn, col) outcomes[[col]][outcomes$outcome == o & outcomes$contrast == cn]

# A causal graph drawn from the coordinates stored in a dagitty object, with
# ggplot2 alone, without ggdag. Observed nodes are filled boxes, latent ones
# outlined; arrows are shortened at both ends so that they stop at the boxes.
dag_plot <- function(g, gap = 0.3) {
  xy <- dagitty::coordinates(g)
  nodes <- tibble::tibble(name = names(xy$x), x = unname(xy$x), y = unname(xy$y)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(latent = name %in% dagitty::latents(g))
  arrows <- tibble::as_tibble(dagitty::edges(g)[, c("v", "w")]) |>
    dplyr::left_join(nodes |> dplyr::select(v = "name", x0 = "x", y0 = "y"), by = "v") |>
    dplyr::left_join(nodes |> dplyr::select(w = "name", x1 = "x", y1 = "y"), by = "w") |>
    dplyr::mutate(len = sqrt((x1 - x0)^2 + (y1 - y0)^2),
           xs = x0 + (x1 - x0) * gap / len, ys = y0 + (y1 - y0) * gap / len,
           xe = x1 - (x1 - x0) * gap / len, ye = y1 - (y1 - y0) * gap / len)
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_segment(data = arrows, ggplot2::aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye), colour = "#6c757d",
                 linewidth = 0.6, arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
    ggplot2::geom_label(data = dplyr::filter(nodes, !latent), ggplot2::aes(x, y, label = name), fill = "#00205b",
               colour = "white", size = 3.6, fontface = "bold", linewidth = 0,
               label.padding = grid::unit(5, "pt")) +
    ggplot2::geom_label(data = dplyr::filter(nodes, latent), ggplot2::aes(x, y, label = name), fill = "white",
               colour = "#00205b", size = 3.6, fontface = "bold.italic", linewidth = 0.5,
               linetype = "dashed", label.padding = grid::unit(5, "pt")) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.5)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.35)) +
    ggplot2::theme_void()
}
```

Causal graphs are introduced in this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) through the Housing and racial bias case study, as are the consequences of restricting a comparison to the cases in which a common effect took one value. Sections 1 to 6 draw the causal graphs of the case study and derive from these graphs what an analysis has to hold constant and what it must leave alone. The graph drawn in section 4 is the graph of Task 2, the same in the workspace, in the deck and in the browser lab as on this page. Section 7 considers what the data can and cannot establish about a graph, before section 8 turns to a graph of your own. The case study rests on a field experiment, described on the [background page](../background.qmd), in which the original authors emailed public housing authorities from six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. Task 2 of the exercise asks you to finish a graph of the case study, which this module builds step by step with the R package dagitty, the package that answers the questions in the workspace. The deck and the browser lab print the same answers from a table computed by the course with dagitty, since the package cannot run in a browser. The code is shown, and every number concerning the case study is computed from the course files in `data/` when the page is built.

## 1. Arrows as claims {#sec-arrows}

A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, is a picture of what you believe causes what. *Directed* means that every edge is an arrow, whose head is the effect, and *acyclic* that you cannot follow the arrows out of a variable and come back to it. The graph comes before the model, stating the assumptions about the world from which the regression follows, and an analyst who has named the quantity that the analysis is for, the estimand, can thus derive from the graph which variables to hold constant [@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand; @HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat].

The Housing case study begins with the smallest graph possible, in which the name on an email may affect the greeting of the reply and nothing else in the graph causes the name, since the name was assigned by a random number generator. In the language of dagitty the graph is a short text, with one line per arrow, in which the exposure and the outcome are marked so that the package knows which effect is being asked about.

```{r}
#| label: first-dag
first <- dagitty::dagitty('dag {
  name [exposure, pos="0,0"]
  greeting [outcome, pos="2,0"]
  name -> greeting
}')
dagitty::adjustmentSets(first)
```

`adjustmentSets()` returns the sets of variables that have to be held constant for the effect of the exposure on the outcome to be estimated, and here it returns the empty set, written `{}`, meaning that nothing needs adjusting. That is what random assignment secures, in that no arrow can point into the name, and no other cause of the greeting can therefore also have shaped which name an authority received.

## 2. Confounder, mediator, collider {#sec-shapes}

Most decisions about adjustment come down to recognising one of three arrangements of three variables, drawn in @fig-shapes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shapes
#| fig-cap: "Three arrangements of three variables. Left, z is a common cause of x and y (a confounder); centre, m lies on the path from x to y (a mediator); right, c is a common effect of x and y (a collider)."
#| fig-alt: "Three small graphs side by side. In the first, z points to both x and y and x points to y. In the second, x points to m and m points to y. In the third, x and y both point to c."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.2
shapes <- list(
  confounder = dagitty::dagitty('dag { x [pos="0,0"] y [pos="2,0"] z [pos="1,1"] z -> x z -> y x -> y }'),
  mediator = dagitty::dagitty('dag { x [pos="0,0"] y [pos="2,0"] m [pos="1,1"] x -> m m -> y }'),
  collider = dagitty::dagitty('dag { x [pos="0,0"] y [pos="2,0"] c [pos="1,-1"] x -> c y -> c }')
)
purrr::imap(shapes, \(g, nm) dag_plot(g, gap = 0.22) + ggplot2::labs(title = nm)) |>
  patchwork::wrap_plots(nrow = 1)
```

A **confounder** is a common cause of the exposure and the outcome, and such a variable opens a path between the two that has nothing to do with the effect. The plain association therefore mixes the effect with the confounding, and adjusting for the confounder closes that path. Had the original authors compared emails that applicants happened to send, rather than names assigned by the authors, the composition of a community could have shaped both who wrote and how officials answered, and it would have been a confounder, whereas random assignment removes every such path at once.

A **mediator** lies on the path from the exposure to the outcome and transmits part of the effect. Whether to adjust for a mediator depends on which quantity is wanted, the mediator being left alone for the total effect and held constant only if the target is the part of the effect that does not run through it.

A **collider** is a common effect of two variables. Left alone, a collider blocks the path between its two causes and leaves these causes unrelated, whereas holding it constant opens the path and creates an association between causes that had none. Restricting a sample to the cases in which the collider took one value has the same effect as putting it in the model, selecting on a variable thus amounting to conditioning on it, a mechanism that has produced spurious findings in several literatures [@ColeEtAl2010IllustratingBiasDue; @GriffithEtAl2020ColliderBiasUndermines].

## 3. Conditioning on a reply {#sec-collider}

In the Housing case study it is the reply that needs care. Whether an official replies may depend on the name, and it surely also depends on the official, on workload, habits and the way in which the office handles email, none of which is recorded in the data. A reply is therefore a common effect of the name and of the official's traits, a collider, and a comparison of greetings among the replies is a comparison restricted to one value of that collider.

The quickest way of finding out what such a restriction does is to build data in which the answer is known, and the simulation below writes a world in which the name lowers the chance of a reply but has *no* effect at all on how a reply begins. Each official has one unrecorded trait, whose effect differs between the three worlds. In the first world the trait makes both a reply and a named greeting more likely, in the second it makes a reply more likely and a named greeting less likely, and in the third it affects only the greeting.

```{r}
#| label: collider-sim
simulate_housing <- function(trait_on_reply, trait_on_greeting, n = 1e5, seed = 20261025) {
  set.seed(seed)
  tibble::tibble(hisp = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), trait = rnorm(n)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      reply = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.3 + trait_on_reply * trait - 0.8 * hisp)),
      # the name does not appear here: it has no effect on the greeting
      greeting = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.4 + trait_on_greeting * trait)),
      named_reply = reply * greeting
    )
}
gap <- \(y, hisp) 100 * (mean(y[hisp == 1]) - mean(y[hisp == 0]))

settings <- tibble::tibble(
  setting = c("the trait raises replies and greetings", "the trait raises replies, lowers greetings",
              "the trait affects greetings only"),
  trait_on_reply = c(1.5, 1.5, 0),
  trait_on_greeting = c(1.5, -1.5, 1.5)
)
sim_results <- settings |>
  datawizard::data_modify(sim = purrr::map2(trait_on_reply, trait_on_greeting, simulate_housing),
         gap_replies = purrr::map_dbl(sim, \(d) d |> dplyr::filter(reply == 1) |> dplyr::summarise(g = gap(greeting, hisp)) |> dplyr::pull(g)),
         gap_all_emails = purrr::map_dbl(sim, \(d) gap(d$named_reply, d$hisp))) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("setting", "gap_replies", "gap_all_emails"))
sim_results |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1)))
```

In none of the three worlds does the name change how a reply begins, yet the comparison among the replies finds a gap of `r fmt(sim_results$gap_replies[1])` points in the first, `r fmt(sim_results$gap_replies[2])` in the second and `r fmt(sim_results$gap_replies[3])` in the third. When the trait raises replies, the officials who still reply to a discouraging name are, on average, further along the trait than those who reply to the other name, and whatever the trait does to the greeting appears as a gap between the names. The direction of the spurious gap depends on how the trait acts on the greeting, which the graph does not specify. The third world illustrates the converse case, in which a trait that does not affect the reply leaves the replies to the two names alike and the comparison among these replies clean. The comparison among all emails, in which an email without a reply counts as one without a named greeting, finds gaps of `r fmt(sim_results$gap_all_emails[1])`, `r fmt(sim_results$gap_all_emails[2])` and `r fmt(sim_results$gap_all_emails[3])` points, and rightly so, because in these worlds the name does change the chance of receiving a named reply, by discouraging the reply itself, the size of that change depending on how many replies each world produces.

The simulation makes the name reduce replies far more sharply than in the real data, to make the effect easy to detect. In the experiment itself, emails with Hispanic names drew a reply `r fmt(abs(out("reply", "hispanic", "b_pp")))` points less often than emails with white names, and the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) shows how far a selection of that size could shift the comparison among replies.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

In the `collider-sim` chunk, set the effect of the name on the reply from −0.8 to 0, so that the name no longer discourages replies, and rerun it. What happens to the gap among the replies in the first two worlds, and why? Then add an arrow `name -> greeting` to the simulation, with a coefficient of −0.5 on the logit of the greeting, and see how the gap among the replies now mixes the true effect with the selection.
:::

## 4. The graph of the case study {#sec-case}

@fig-case draws the case study as Task 2 asks for it, with the name possibly affecting both the reply and the greeting, and with an arrow from the reply into the greeting, since the reply comes before any greeting. The official's traits, which the data do not record, affect both whether the official replies and whether a reply opens with the name, as do the characteristics of the community, recorded in the public file as thirds, and the graph marks the official as latent, meaning unobserved.

```{r}
#| label: case-dag
case_graph <- dagitty::dagitty('dag {
  name [exposure, pos="2,2.8"]
  greeting [outcome, pos="4,1"]
  reply [pos="0,1"]
  community [pos="2,1.75"]
  official [latent, pos="2,0.15"]
  name -> reply
  name -> greeting
  reply -> greeting
  community -> reply
  community -> greeting
  official -> reply
  official -> greeting
}')
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-case
#| fig-cap: "The Housing case study as a graph. The name and the community each point into the reply and the greeting, and so do the traits of the official who reads the email, which the data do not record (dashed)."
#| fig-alt: "A graph with name at the top, reply on the left, greeting on the right and community in the middle, each of name and community pointing to reply and greeting; reply points to greeting; official, drawn dashed at the bottom, points to reply and greeting."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
dag_plot(case_graph)
```

`paths()` lists every route between the exposure and the outcome, whatever the direction of its arrows, and reports whether each route is open. Asked again with `Z = "reply"`, the function indicates which routes are open once the reply is held constant, as it is in a comparison among replies.

```{r}
#| label: case-paths
dagitty::paths(case_graph)
dagitty::paths(case_graph, Z = "reply")
```

Left alone, two routes are open, the direct arrow from the name to the greeting and the route through the reply, both of which belong to the effect of the name, while the routes through the community and through the official are closed, since they pass the reply as a collider. Conditioning on the reply reverses this pattern, closing the route through the reply, which is the point of comparing among replies, while opening the two routes that pass the reply as a collider. These two routes carry an association between the name and the greeting that lies outside the effect of the name.

The comparison among replies aims at the direct effect of the name, the part of its effect on the greeting that does not run through the reply, and dagitty can be asked for an adjustment set for that quantity.

```{r}
#| label: case-direct
direct_sets <- dagitty::adjustmentSets(case_graph, effect = "direct")
length(direct_sets)   # the number of sets that identify the direct effect
observed <- case_graph
dagitty::latents(observed) <- character(0)
dagitty::adjustmentSets(observed, effect = "direct")
```

With the official's traits unobserved, dagitty returns no set at all, meaning that no adjustment permitted by the data identifies the direct effect. If the traits could be measured, the set would comprise the reply, the community and the official together. The community thirds close one of the two routes that conditioning opens, which is a reason to prefer an adjusted comparison among replies to a raw one, although the route through the official remains open whatever is adjusted for.

## 5. Counting all delivered emails {#sec-all-emails}

The other comparison changes the outcome rather than the rows, the outcome for every delivered email being whether a reply came that opened with the sender's name, with an email without a reply counting as 0. This comparison was chosen by the analyst 25N5D, following @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias, and is mentioned by the original authors in a footnote. On the graph the new outcome is a single node into which both the reply and the greeting point.

```{r}
#| label: all-dag
all_emails <- dagitty::dagitty('dag {
  name [exposure]
  named_reply [outcome]
  official [latent]
  name -> reply -> named_reply
  name -> greeting -> named_reply
  community -> reply
  community -> greeting
  official -> reply
  official -> greeting
}')
dagitty::adjustmentSets(all_emails)
dagitty::isAdjustmentSet(all_emails, "community")
```

The minimal adjustment set is empty again, and since `isAdjustmentSet()` confirms that adding the community keeps the estimate valid, the community may be added for precision. As every route from the name to the named reply runs forward through the reply or the greeting, and nothing is conditioned on, the comparison of all delivered emails estimates the total effect of the name on receiving a named reply exactly as randomisation set it up. The price lies in the outcome, which combines whether a reply came with how it began and thus answers a related question rather than the question of tone posed by the claim. On the data the two comparisons yield `r fmt(out("named", "hispanic", "b_pp"))` points among the replies and `r fmt(out("named_any", "hispanic", "b_pp"))` among all delivered emails, and the specification curve retains both as two estimands.

## 6. The adjustment sets of the curve {#sec-adjustment}

The graph also explains the decision about adjustment taken on the curve, whose covariates, the hard-to-find address and the community thirds, were all fixed before the emails went out. None of these covariates can therefore be a mediator or a descendant of the name, and none of them is a confounder, since nothing points into the name. For the comparison of all delivered emails the covariates secure precision and nothing else, and adding them changes little. Among the replies the covariates do one more thing, because the community thirds close one of the routes opened by the conditioning.

```{r}
#| label: adjust-shift
curve |>
  datawizard::data_filter(model == "lpm", uncoded == "drop", comparison == "white") |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("population", "adjust", "b_pp", "n")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(b_pp = round(b_pp, 2))
```

Among the replies, the adjustment for the community shifts the gap from `r curve |> dplyr::filter(model == "lpm", uncoded == "drop", comparison == "white", population == "replies", adjust == "none") |> dplyr::pull(b_pp) |> fmt()` to `r curve |> dplyr::filter(model == "lpm", uncoded == "drop", comparison == "white", population == "replies", adjust == "place_ethnic") |> dplyr::pull(b_pp) |> fmt()` points, and among all delivered emails from `r curve |> dplyr::filter(model == "lpm", uncoded == "drop", comparison == "white", population == "all", adjust == "none") |> dplyr::pull(b_pp) |> fmt()` to `r curve |> dplyr::filter(model == "lpm", uncoded == "drop", comparison == "white", population == "all", adjust == "place_ethnic") |> dplyr::pull(b_pp) |> fmt()`. Part of each shift comes from the `r no_thirds` emails without community thirds, which are excluded from the adjusted specifications, and part from chance differences between the groups, and the numbers therefore cannot show how much selection the adjustment removes. The graph indicates only that the adjustment removes some selection, and that it cannot remove the part that runs through the official.

The sex of the name and the ethnicity of the official who replied, two further decisions on the menu, occupy different places on the graph. The sex of the name is part of the treatment and was crossed with the group by design, which means that it confounds nothing and that adjusting for it serves as a check. Whether the official who replied had a Hispanic name is known only for replies, which makes this variable a descendant of the collider, and a comparison within the replies from such officials conditions on the reply and on what came after it, which is why the menu treats that subgroup as another question.

## 7. Graphs and data {#sec-quartet}

No statistic computed from the Housing data can establish whether the route through the official is open, or in which direction it bends. @DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot construct four datasets with identical summary statistics, generated by four different causal structures, in which adjusting for the same covariate is right in one and wrong in the others, because what differs between the structures is not contained in the observed variables. The same holds in the present case, where the graph, the reasons behind its arrows and the assumption on which the bound of the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) rests are all claims about the world. An analyst states these claims so that a reader can dispute an arrow, and no output of a model can take their place.

Of the two working rules that follow, both cheap to apply, the first is time order. Nothing that happens after the treatment can be a confounder of it, and a variable recorded after the email arrived, such as the reply or the ethnicity of the official who wrote it, therefore needs a reason before it enters an analysis of the effect of the name. Time order is of less help in a survey, in which several attitudes are recorded in the same interview and the order of the arrows has to rest on an argument about which attitude forms first. The second rule is to include the graph in the report, as the preregistration of Task 5 requires when it asks for a sentence, grounded in the graph, on why the chosen specification answers the claim.

Fit criteria can actively mislead in the choice of a control set, a point made by Katrin Auspurg about a large multiverse of political-science models, in which the AIC comparison reported in the study itself systematically favours the specifications that she classes as unjustified [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. A model that adjusts for a collider will often fit better than one that does not, because the collider genuinely predicts the outcome. Predictive performance is a poor guide to a control set, even though it is often the guide that analysts follow without saying so. For the first of the two rules, `ggdag::time_ordered_coords()` lays a graph out in temporal layers, making visible on the page any arrow that runs backwards in time.

A four-step procedure covers most first graphs. State the estimand in words – the quantity, for which units, contrasting what with what. List every variable that you believe is causally involved as a node of the graph, including the ones you cannot measure. Draw the arrows you would defend and comment out the ones you would not. Then read the adjustment set, and write the model formula from it. The [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd#sec-auspurg) takes up the argument from that point, since a graph is what the critics of large specification universes ask analysts to supply.

## 8. Your own graph {#sec-yours}

The exercise for this section uses a question from your own research in place of the Housing case study, and it has two halves.

First, state an estimand for a question you actually care about, in one or two sentences and in the vocabulary of @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand. Name the unit of analysis, the outcome, the contrast that defines the effect, and the population over which you want it.

Second, draw it. The graphs of sections 1 to 6 are written as dagitty text, and a graph of your own is easier to revise when each arrow is an ordinary formula, as in `ggdag::dagify()` from the **ggdag** package. The outcome goes on the left of the tilde and its causes on the right, as in `lm()`, so `greeting ~ name` reads 'the name causes the greeting'. A formula is an R expression, so a `#` in front of one comments the arrow out and the call still parses, and `dagify()` returns a dagitty object, so the queries of sections 1 to 6 work on it unchanged. Open a script and write a `ggdag::dagify()` call with one formula per arrow. Include the variables you cannot measure, because their absence from your data does not remove them from the world and the graph is where that fact becomes visible. Comment out the arrows you are unsure of, then run `adjustmentSets()` twice, once with them and once without, and see whether your model changes. Write the formula that the set implies and compare it with the model you were going to fit anyway.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Do the exercise above on the last analysis you ran, not on a hypothetical one. Then find the control variable in that model that would be hardest to defend in a seminar, put it on the graph, and work out which of the three shapes it is. If it turns out to be a collider, or a mediator in a model you reported as a total effect, you have learned something that could not be read from the model output.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The estimand-first framing comes from @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand, and the standard treatment of causal graphs for social scientists is @HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat, which is freely available online, while @Huntington-Klein2021EffectIntroductionResearch offers a gentler introduction to the three shapes. On colliders, @ColeEtAl2010IllustratingBiasDue give the general treatment, @ElwertWinship2014EndogenousSelectionBias the treatment for sociologists, with selection into a sample as the leading case, and @GriffithEtAl2020ColliderBiasUndermines a widely read applied example, while conditioning after the treatment in experiments is treated by @MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment, with @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias for audit studies. The demonstration that no statistic chooses an adjustment set is due to @DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot. The software documentation is worth reading directly: the ggdag package site at <https://r-causal.github.io/ggdag/>, whose introductory vignette pictures association flowing along a path as water flows down a pipe, and the dagitty documentation at <https://dagitty.net/>, which also hosts a browser tool for sketching a graph by hand before writing it down. The numbers reported for the Housing case study come from `display_outcomes.csv`, `spec_curve.csv` and `housing_emails.csv` in `data/`.
